title: Yield and atom economy - 123 school
heading: Yield and atom economy
intro: These questions are about excess, yield, atom economy and the E-factor.
Test your knowledge by typing your answer and comparing it with the correct answer. Then click 'Check answers'.

questions.q: What is a limiting reactant?
questions.a: The starting substance that is used up first; it determines how much product is formed

questions.q: What is a substance in excess?
questions.a: A starting substance of which some is left after the reaction

questions.q: How do you determine which substance is limiting?
questions.a: Convert the amounts to moles and compare them with the mole ratio in the reaction equation

questions.q: You have 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub> and 2.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> for 2 H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O. Which substance is limiting and how many moles of water form?
questions.a: H<sub>2</sub> is limiting (1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> is needed); 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>O forms

questions.q: Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. You have 0.100 mol Zn and 0.50 mol HCl. Which substance is in excess and how many moles of H<sub>2</sub> form?
questions.a: HCl is in excess (only 0.20 mol is needed); 0.100 mol H<sub>2</sub> forms

questions.q: What is the theoretical yield?
questions.a: The amount of product you would get if all of the limiting reactant is converted without any loss

questions.q: Give the formula for the yield (BINAS table 37H)
questions.a: Yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%

questions.q: Why is the yield of a reaction in practice usually lower than 100%?
questions.a: Because of losses (for example during filtering), side reactions and incomplete conversion (equilibrium)

questions.q: The theoretical yield is 25.0 g and you obtain 20.0 g. Calculate the yield
The theoretical yield is 50 g and the yield is 70%. How many grams of product do you obtain?
4.86 g of Mg reacts with excess oxygen: 2 Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2 MgO. Calculate the theoretical yield of MgO (M = 40.30 g/mol)
You obtain 7.25 g of MgO while the theoretical yield is 8.06 g. Calculate the yield
Give the formula for atom economy (BINAS table 37H)
questions.a: Atom economy = (mass of the desired product according to the reaction equation / total mass of the starting substances according to the reaction equation) × 100%

questions.q: What does the atom economy tell you?
questions.a: What part of the mass of the starting substances ends up in the desired product

questions.q: What is the difference between yield and atom economy?
questions.a: Yield tells how much product you really get compared with theory; atom economy tells how much of the starting substances ends up in the desired product in principle, even if the reaction goes to completion

questions.q: What is the atom economy of an addition reaction, such as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>?
questions.a: 100%, because all atoms of the starting substances are in the only product

questions.q: Calculate the atom economy for CaO from CaCO<sub>3</sub> → CaO + CO<sub>2</sub> (M: CaCO<sub>3</sub> 100.09, CaO 56.08 g/mol)
Calculate the atom economy for ethanol in C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2 CO<sub>2</sub> (M: glucose 180.16, ethanol 46.07 g/mol)
Calculate the atom economy for Fe in Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3 CO → 2 Fe + 3 CO<sub>2</sub> (M: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> 159.69, CO 28.01, Fe 55.85 g/mol)
What is the E-factor (BINAS table 37H)?
questions.a: The mass of waste per mass of desired product (E-factor = mass of waste / mass of product)

questions.q: Is a high or a low E-factor better for the environment?
questions.a: A low E-factor: less waste per kg of product

questions.q: In a process 5.0 kg of product and 20 kg of waste are formed. Calculate the E-factor
From 40.0 g of starting materials 15.7 g of the desired product is formed; the rest is waste. Calculate the E-factor
Name three principles of green chemistry
questions.a: For example: prevent waste, high atom economy, use catalysts, less hazardous substances, renewable raw materials, save energy

questions.q: In which BINAS table do you find the principles of green chemistry?
questions.a: Table 97F

questions.q: Why is a catalyst good for green chemistry?
questions.a: A catalyst makes reactions possible at a lower temperature (less energy) and is not used up

questions.q: What is the difference between a batch process and a continuous process?
questions.a: In a batch process you make one portion of product at a time (fill, react, empty); in a continuous process starting materials are fed in all the time and product comes out all the time

questions.q: Why is a closed cycle (reusing substances) good for green chemistry?
questions.a: Less raw material is lost and less waste is formed
